briefing.opening: Good morning/afternoon. I will now begin the climate briefing for August 10, 2026.

sections.title: 🔴 Unprecedented Heatwaves and Marine Heatwaves, Deepening Climate Crisis
sections.content: Last month, global ocean temperatures reached an all-time high, with marine heatwaves impacting the entire planet [13, 17, 58]. Specifically, in France, water use restrictions due to heatwaves and drought have been implemented across 70% of the country [15, 16, 20, 22], and the UK also saw three-quarters of its land in drought conditions, with Europe as a whole experiencing a fierce summer [24, 59, 88, 91]. In the Pacific Northwest of the United States, historic wildfires have erupted, destroying hundreds of buildings, leading to 'unprecedented and dangerous situations' [95], demonstrating the devastating reality of climate change threatening a generation [72, 78].

sections.title: ⚠️ Direct Impact of Climate Change: Visible Domestic and International Economic and Social Damages
sections.content: Climate change is already causing immense losses across domestic and international economies and societies. Hanwha Life Insurance anticipates climate change-related losses to reach 2.2 trillion won by 2050 and is accelerating preparations for phased asset management [3], with active discussions also underway regarding the new role of insurance amidst climate disasters like torrential rains [5]. The domestic protected horticulture sector has been directly hit by climate change, urgently requiring customized technology adoption strategies for each crop type [4], and the 'Climate Insurance Act' for compensating crop damage due to heatwaves has passed a subcommittee of the Special Committee on Climate, highlighting the urgent need for damage compensation measures [10]. Furthermore, safety issues such as increased electricity demand due to heatwaves and vehicle fires are continuously occurring [19, 54, 57], and widespread damages are becoming visible, including threats to Italy's Parmigiano cheese production [61].

sections.title: 🌱 Accelerating Efforts for Carbon Neutrality and Renewable Energy Transition
sections.content: Globally, efforts to achieve carbon neutrality and transition to renewable energy are accelerating. Australia has fully launched its net-zero national strategy [9]; domestically, Jincheon County is spurring the realization of carbon neutrality and the promotion of energy welfare, while Gwangmyeong City is expanding the use of electronic receipts with small business owners, spreading carbon neutrality practices [27, 31, 33, 34]. Furthermore, renewable energy projects are being actively pursued, such as Korea Southern Power (KOSPO) commencing construction of the nation's largest 400MW solar power plant in Haenam [45, 49], and EREIM has acquired 100% of Wonpick E&C's shares to fully embark on new and renewable energy businesses [35, 40]. APEC has also agreed to jointly respond to extreme weather events such as 42.5-degree heatwaves and strong El Niño phenomena, strengthening international cooperation [18, 21].

sections.title: 🇰🇷 Strengthening Domestic Climate Change Response Capabilities and Raising Awareness
sections.content: Domestically, various efforts are being made to raise awareness of climate change and strengthen response capabilities. The Korea Meteorological Administration successfully concluded the '3rd Climate Change Science Quiz Competition,' encouraging the cultivation of climate knowledge among future generations [2, 6], and approximately 500 rural leaders in the Yesan region gathered to commit to the future of local agriculture amidst climate change [1]. The Rural Development Administration is also striving to develop adaptation technologies, such as preventing climate change-related pest and disease damage through research on African insects [14], and the National Climate Crisis Response Committee is leading international climate governance discussions, expanding Korea's role [12]. However, alongside criticism regarding the ambiguity of industrial greenhouse gas reduction targets [26, 28, 55], an analysis suggesting that additional carbon reductions can be achieved with existing plans has been raised [56], thus, the development of more realistic and proactive reduction strategies is required.

briefing.closing: In today's briefing, we have examined the unprecedented climate crisis, its resulting domestic and international damages, and the various efforts and challenges in confronting it. Climate change is no longer a future problem but a present threat, demanding immediate and integrated responses. This concludes today's climate briefing.
